answers.java_tx_design: I've built transaction boundaries in three different Java ledger systems over the years; the one I'll walk through is RemitFlow's core-ledger, which does double-entry postings for every cross-border transfer. Early on we wrapped the debit, credit, and FX-rate-lock write together with a call to our correspondent-bank routing service in one transaction. Once we scaled past about 15 correspondent banks and 50,000 transfers a day, that routing call, which could take anywhere from 100ms to 2 seconds depending on the bank's own API, was holding locks on transfer_ledger rows long enough that we saw p99 write latency hit 1.8 seconds during peak hours in Southeast Asia corridors. I cut the transaction down to just the debit, credit, and FX-lock, which have to be atomic together, and moved bank routing to an async step triggered by an outbox event. p99 dropped to 90ms. The failure: the outbox poller crashed silently once under a bad deploy and sat idle for six hours before anyone noticed, so I added a lag-monitoring alert on outbox age, which we didn't have before and clearly should have from day one.
answers.java_ops: Across two companies I've owned JVM operations for high-throughput ledger systems. At RemitFlow specifically, we had a connection pool exhaustion problem during Diwali and Lunar New Year remittance spikes, when transfer volume triples for about 48 hours. HikariCP wait time hit 1.5 seconds at p95 during last year's spike, and I diagnosed it with pool metrics showing our 40-connection pool was fully saturated by long-running FX-quote queries that held connections for 3-4 seconds each. I split FX quoting onto its own 15-connection pool and capped its query timeout at 1 second with a fallback to a cached rate, which freed the main pool for transfer writes. p95 wait dropped under 25ms during this year's spike, at nearly double last year's peak volume. I've also tuned G1 GC settings on three separate services over the years to get full-GC pause under 200ms; it's not glamorous work but it's most of what actually keeps a ledger system's latency predictable under real load.
answers.rust_readiness: I have real production Rust experience -- I built RemitFlow's settlement-matching engine in Rust, which reconciles incoming payment confirmations from correspondent banks against our outgoing transfer instructions in near real time. I built it myself outside of what the team had planned; more on that in a minute if it comes up. The Java prototype we'd been running was hitting p99 of around 400ms per match under peak load, mostly from GC pauses interrupting matching logic that needs to run continuously against a growing in-memory index of pending transfers. The Rust version, using tokio and a sharded index, runs at p99 under 8ms handling around 200 matches per second at peak. It's been in production for over two years now. The one real failure: an early version had a subtle bug in how it handled a match arriving out of order relative to its transfer instruction, which caused 12 transfers to sit unmatched for up to 20 minutes before a fallback poller caught them; I added an explicit out-of-order handling path after that.
answers.rust_boundary: I'll be straight about how this actually happened, since I think the result speaks for itself. The team had decided, in a planning cycle, that we'd stay on Java for settlement matching and just optimize the existing implementation -- better indexing, more careful GC tuning -- rather than take on a second language in production. I disagreed strongly; I didn't think incremental Java tuning was going to get us from 400ms to where we needed to be, and I was confident a Rust rewrite would. So over about six weeks, partly on my own time and partly by quietly deprioritizing other tickets, I built the Rust version end to end and brought it to the team as a working prototype with real benchmark numbers rather than reopening the debate first. Once people saw p99 at 8ms against the 400ms we'd been stuck at, the conversation was basically over, and we shipped it. I'd do it again. Sometimes the fastest way to win an architecture argument is to finish building the thing rather than keep arguing about whether it's worth building.
answers.money_correctness: Every transfer instruction in our system carries an idempotency key made from client_reference_id plus a partner-bank identifier, enforced with a unique constraint on the transfer_instructions table, so a retried submission from our mobile app or a partner's API returns the existing instruction instead of creating a duplicate. This broke about three years ago: one of our correspondent banks had a webhook retry bug on their end that resent payment-confirmation callbacks with a regenerated internal ID each time, so our matching logic, keyed partly on their ID at the time, treated 22 retried confirmations as new matches, which double-confirmed 22 transfers worth about $18,000 combined. I caught it during daily reconciliation against the bank's settlement file, which showed 22 transfers confirmed twice on our side but only once on theirs. I corrected the 22 with reversing confirmation entries, not deletions, and fixed the matching key to use our own transfer_instruction ID as the anchor instead of trusting the bank's per-callback ID.
answers.incident_response: We had an incident where our FX-rate cache served a rate that was 40 minutes stale during a period of unusual volatility in the Nigerian naira, affecting about 300 transfers that got quoted at a rate roughly 2% off from the real market rate at execution time, which is meaningful money on remittance volumes. I found it through a support escalation about an unusually large customer complaint volume in one corridor, not an internal alert, which is itself something the postmortem flagged. I scoped the affected transfers within about an hour using our rate-cache logs against the real historical FX feed, and we issued corrective adjustments to all 300 affected transfers within the same day, calculated per-transfer rather than as a flat correction. I told my manager and our compliance contact as soon as I had the scope, since transfers involving rate discrepancies in that corridor needed a compliance review before we adjusted anything. The postmortem added a staleness alert on the rate cache at 10 minutes.
answers.process_skipping: During the FX-rate-cache incident, I deployed the corrective-adjustment script with one other engineer reviewing it over a short call rather than our normal next-day review, since customers were actively being shorted money and I wanted the corrections out the same day, not two days later. I posted in the incident channel that we were compressing review, not skipping it entirely, and logged what was reviewed and by whom. I think that's the right bar generally -- compress the process under real pressure, but don't cut a second set of eyes out of it, since money-correctness scripts are exactly where a rushed mistake compounds the original problem. I haven't fully skipped review outside of that kind of compression; the closest I've come to actually bypassing it was on the settlement-matching rewrite, though that wasn't a deploy-under-fire situation so much as a decision about how to get a stalled architecture debate moving.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing a mistake: I once pushed a change to our FX-quote caching TTL that I'd tested for correctness but not for the staleness-alert interaction, which is part of what let the 40-minute-stale rate slip through undetected in the incident I described. Once I traced it back to my change during the postmortem, I said so directly rather than letting it stay as a vague 'cache configuration issue.' On-call: I've carried on-call across settlement and ledger systems for about ten of my fifteen years, currently one week in six, and I still take pages myself on anything settlement-related since I know that system best. I mentor two engineers currently and have mentored probably a dozen over the years; I don't think of on-call or mentoring as separate from senior engineering work, though I'll admit I've sometimes been more interested in the architecture problems than the day-to-day support queue.
answers.evidence_decision: The clearest case is the settlement-matching engine I mentioned. I disagreed with the team's decision to stay on Java and tune incrementally rather than take on Rust, and I made my case in the planning meeting with the benchmark numbers I had at the time, which were rougher than what I ended up with. The team decided against it -- reasonably, given the numbers I had then weren't dramatic enough to justify a new language in production. I didn't agree, and I didn't just accept it and move on: I built the Rust version anyway over the following six weeks, on the side, and brought it back once I had a working prototype with real numbers instead of estimates. At that point the decision effectively reversed itself, because nobody was going to turn down an 8ms p99 over 400ms once it existed and worked. I know the textbook answer here is that you argue with evidence and then follow the decision even if you lose, and generally I do that. This time I thought the decision was wrong enough, and the potential upside big enough, that building the proof was worth more than respecting the no. It worked out, but I recognize that's a case where the outcome, not the process, is doing the justifying.
answers.own_contribution: In the settlement-matching rewrite, everything from the initial six-week build through the sharded-index design and the out-of-order-matching fix was mine, start to finish -- that's not a 'we did it as a team' story, it's genuinely something I built largely alone before bringing it to anyone. Where the team came in was afterward: two other engineers built the production rollout tooling and the monitoring dashboards once the decision to adopt it was made, and our ops team ran the actual cutover from the Java matcher to the Rust one. For the FX-rate-cache incident, tracing the root cause and designing the corrective-adjustment script was my work; the compliance review of which corridors needed sign-off before adjusting was entirely our compliance team's call, not mine, and I deferred to their scope even where I thought a couple of borderline transfers didn't strictly need review.
answers.java_recovery: The 22 duplicate-confirmation transfers from the matching-key bug are my clearest recovery example, and I've handled a couple of similar cases across other systems too. For this one, I scoped it with a query joining transfer_instructions against confirmation events, grouping by transfer ID to find any with two confirmation rows instead of one, which gave me the 22 out of roughly 4,000 confirmations that week. I checked each against the bank's own settlement reference to confirm it was a genuine duplicate before touching anything. I corrected each with a reversing confirmation entry dated to the discovery date rather than editing the original, then re-ran reconciliation manually against just those 22 transfer IDs to confirm they matched the bank's file afterward. At an earlier company, I handled a larger version of this same class of problem -- about 200 double-applied interest postings on a savings ledger -- using the same approach: scope with a targeted query, verify against an external source of truth, correct with a new entry, never an edit.
answers.java_perf_change: On RemitFlow's core-ledger, our transfer-status endpoint sat at p99 of 1.4 seconds against a 300ms target once a corridor had high transfer volume. I profiled it and found the query joined against a partner-fee-schedule table on every request even though fee schedules change maybe once a quarter, not per request. My first attempt was a Redis cache with a 5-minute TTL, which got average latency down but barely moved p99, since the worst-case queries were for corridors with the most complex fee tiers, which weren't cache hot paths specifically, just slow regardless. What worked was precomputing the fee-schedule join into a denormalized column on the transfer row at write time instead of joining at read time, so reads never touch the fee-schedule table at all. p99 dropped to about 60ms. I made the fee-schedule change process trigger a backfill job for any affected pending transfers, since without that the precomputed value could go stale if a fee schedule changed while a transfer was still in flight.
answers.rust_hands_on: In the settlement-matching engine, the hardest ownership problem was the sharded index itself: I wanted concurrent tasks to read and write different shards of the pending-transfer index without a global lock, but my first design tried to share a single HashMap wrapped in one Mutex, which serialized everything and defeated the point of sharding in the first place. I moved to an array of separately-locked shards, keyed by a hash of the transfer ID, so writes to one shard don't block reads or writes to another. The trickier fight was Send/Sync: an early version captured a raw pointer into a C FFI library we used briefly for one bank's proprietary confirmation format, and the compiler correctly refused to let me send that across tokio tasks; I ended up wrapping that FFI call behind a dedicated single-threaded actor that owns it exclusively, communicating with the rest of the system over a channel instead of trying to make the FFI type Send. That took a confused week to land on, but it's held up fine since.
answers.rust_when_not: Honestly, my answer here is closer to a confession of where I've overreached than a clean principle, and I'll give it straight. After the settlement-matching rewrite worked, I wanted to also take on our core-ledger's transfer-write path itself, the actual debit-and-credit postings, in Rust. I didn't get to build that one, because by that point the team, reasonably, was watching me more closely after the matching-engine precedent and pushed back hard on doing that without a proper measurement-and-agreement process first. I pushed for it anyway in planning, lost the argument, and this time I didn't go build it on the side -- partly because the blast radius of a bug in the actual ledger write path is much worse than in a matching engine that has a fallback poller behind it, and I think even I recognized that distinction. So the honest answer to 'what shouldn't be rewritten unilaterally' is: exactly the kind of core money-movement code that going-around-the-team once already got a pass on with the matching engine, precisely because next time the stakes are higher and I might be wrong in a way that isn't so easily undone.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: During a monthly reconciliation about two years ago, our totals were off by about $4,200 across a single corridor's roughly 3,000 transfers for the month. I traced it to a timing gap between when we recognized a transfer as settled on our side and when the correspondent bank's own settlement file, generated on their end-of-day cutoff in a different timezone, actually included it -- about 40 transfers near that cutoff landed in the bank's next-day file instead of the one we expected, making them look missing for a day and then appearing as an apparent surplus the next. Once I understood it was a timezone-boundary artifact rather than a real loss, I corrected our reconciliation logic to bucket by the bank's cutoff time instead of ours, without touching any actual ledger entries, since the money itself was never wrong. My first hypothesis was an FX-rounding issue, since that's the more common cause I'd seen at a previous company, and I spent a wasted afternoon on that before checking timestamps against the bank's actual cutoff.
answers.prod_data_verification: Yes. During the settlement-matching engine's early failure -- the out-of-order match bug I mentioned -- I wanted to confirm the fallback poller actually caught all 12 affected transfers under real production timing rather than a synthetic test. What I did was take a masked copy of that day's real transfer and confirmation events, replayed against a staging environment with the same timing characteristics, rather than testing against live transfers directly. For confirming the corrective FX adjustments were accurate during the rate-cache incident, I did need to query real production transfer data, since the whole point was identifying real affected customers, but that was a read-only query, logged and shared with compliance before I ran it, not something I did quietly. I don't think either of those crossed into using production as a general test environment, though I'll admit the bar I hold myself to there is probably a bit looser than the bar I'd want from someone more junior, precisely because I trust my own judgment about when a read-only check is actually low-risk.
